sections.html: Champaign County covers about 998 square miles of flat farmland and two linked cities, Champaign and Urbana, which nearly wrap around the University of Illinois campus. Urbana is the county seat. The estimate for mid-2025 is 209,972 residents, and 54.0% of homes are lived in by their owners. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $211,500. Those numbers describe the whole county, so a farmhouse east of I-57 and a campus-area duplex can look nothing alike on a tax bill. Price from nearby sales, and treat the countywide median as background only.

sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Champaign County
sections.html:
Several county offices share the work, and each answers a different question. The Supervisor of Assessments handles value, the Board of Review hears disputes about it, and the Treasurer, who also serves as Collector, bills and collects the money.

  • Supervisor of Assessments: receives the work of the township assessors, mails change notices and processes homestead exemptions. The assessment office number is 217-384-3760.
  • Board of Review: three members appointed by the County Board after passing a state exam. They hear complaints, equalize values between townships and add omitted property to the rolls.
  • Treasurer and Collector: mails roughly 77,000 real estate bills a year and distributes the money to 125 taxing districts. The office number is 217-384-3743.
  • County Clerk: handles redemption of taxes after a tax sale and calculates the rates once every taxing body files its levy.

The Treasurer's office is inside the Scott M. Bennett Administrative Center at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana. Mobile homes are billed on their own, about 3,400 of them, and those bills fall due sixty days after mailing.

Township assessors value property as of January 1 and send their work to the Supervisor of Assessments by June 15. Property is assessed at one-third of market value. When a township's level drifts away from that share, the Supervisor can apply a township multiplier, and those multipliers are published in newspapers and on the county website.

The state Department of Revenue reviews the county's assessments each cycle. If it finds the work properly done, it issues a multiplier of 1.

School districts take the largest slice of a bill. Every taxing body votes its levy by December 31 and files it with the County Clerk, and state law limits most levy increases to growth in assessed value and the consumer price index. Bills go out by May 1. If yours never arrives, you still owe the tax, so phone the Treasurer's office for a second copy.

Bills are usually mailed in early May and are typically due in June and September. A payment postmarked on the due date counts as on time. Check the coupon on your own bill for the current year's dates.

Late payments carry interest of 1.5% a month, or any part of a month, under state law, and a late payment schedule is printed on each coupon. A payment returned for any reason is void, with a $30 charge plus statutory interest. Personal and business checks are accepted through September 30. From October 1 the counter takes only cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks.

  • Pay at a participating local bank listed on the county website.
  • Mail a check payable to Champaign County Collector, with the coupon, to P.O. Box 4306, Springfield, IL 62708-4306.
  • Pay online or by phone at 217-834-8713 with a card or eCheck, using the property's PIN. The processing vendor charges a fee.
  • Pay in person at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana, from 8 in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon, Monday through Friday. A 24-hour drop box sits in the parking lot.

File a complaint with the Board of Review between July 1 and September 10. The board takes complaints and holds hearings in that window. After September 10 its members research values and issue written decisions. Office hours are 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., Monday through Thursday, or by appointment.

The board also represents the county if an appeal moves on to the state Property Tax Appeal Board. Bring paper that supports your number, such as the closing statement from a recent purchase and sales of similar homes nearby.

Exemptions reduce the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied, so they shrink the bill without changing what the house is worth.

Champaign County homeowner exemptions
ExemptionReductionWho qualifies
General homestead (Section 15-175)$6,000Owner's primary residence on January 1 of the assessment year
Senior citizens (Section 15-177)$5,000Owners who turn 65 by the end of the assessment year
Senior assessment freeze (Section 15-172)Holds value at a base yearHousehold income up to $75,000, renewed yearly with proof of income
Persons with disabilities (Section 15-168)$2,000Owners with a qualifying disability
Service-connected disability (Section 15-169)Scaled to the disability rating, up to the full assessed value at 70% or higherOwners with a qualifying service-connected disability

The office does not take faxed or emailed forms, so call to have one mailed. When ownership changes, ask whether the seller's exemption ends and what the buyer must file.

What gets sold is the tax, not the house. In October the Collector mails a delinquent notice by certified mail and publishes the owner's name and amount in the newspaper. Anything still unpaid after 4:30 p.m. on October 29 goes into the annual sale on October 30, where a tax buyer pays the taxes and takes a claim against the property.

After the sale the owner owes the amount sold plus interest at the rate set on sale day. About two weeks later the County Clerk, at 217-384-3722, can quote the redemption figure, and a Take Notice from the Clerk arrives within four months. Redemption is paid to the Clerk, who repays the buyer. State law generally allows 3 years from the sale date, with exceptions spelled out in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. A buyer whose claim is not redeemed can ask the circuit court for a deed.

Look over the closing statement. The Treasurer's office tells buyers and sellers to check closing documents, the title company or the attorney to learn whether tax is owed. Depending on the closing date and when the deed was recorded, the bill can be mailed to the previous owner, who must forward it to the new owner.

If a bill is missing, ask the Treasurer for a duplicate by PIN and confirm whether either installment is still open. If taxes are behind, ask what it takes to clear them before closing, since unpaid taxes head toward the October sale. Whatever remains open for the current year is a closing item to settle with the title company or attorney.

A short list to bring or ask for: the property PIN, the closing date, the date the deed will be recorded, and the buyer's mailing address. With those four items the office can tell you what is paid, what is open and where the next bill will go.

faqs.q: Which office mails Champaign County tax bills?
faqs.a: The County Treasurer, who doubles as Collector, mails them, normally in early May. A missing bill is still the owner's responsibility, and the office at 217-384-3743 issues duplicates.

faqs.q: What is the Champaign County appeal window?
faqs.a: July 1 through September 10, filed with the Board of Review. Members research values after September 10 and then issue written decisions.

faqs.q: Are personal checks taken at the counter after September 30?
faqs.a: No. The last day for a personal or business check is September 30. From October 1 the office accepts cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks in person.

faqs.q: Does a tax sale mean I lose my house?
faqs.a: Not right away. What gets sold is the unpaid tax, and the owner can redeem it through the County Clerk with interest. A court deed enters the picture only after the redemption period passes unused.

faqs.q: How much is the general homestead exemption in Champaign County?
faqs.a: The Assessment Office lists a $6,000 reduction in equalized assessed value for an owner-occupied primary residence. Call 217-384-3760 to have the application mailed.
